acceptance_criteria.criterion: Hash("hunter2") equals the SHA-256 hex of UTF-8 "hunter2spdb_42" exactly (lowercase, 64 chars).
The implementation performs no file or network I/O (verified by inspection / absence of using System.IO and System.Net).
The hasher is registered nowhere yet (DI wiring is WP-016); the type is constructible without arguments.
All three test cases pass under dotnet test.

summary: Created Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher implementing IPasswordHasher: SHA-256 over UTF-8(password + 'spdb_42'), lowercase hex.
Created PasswordHasherTests with 3 test cases: known-vector, determinism, verify-match/mismatch.
27/27 tests pass. Release build clean.

comments.note: SHA256.HashData is a static one-shot API introduced in .NET 6 that avoids allocating a SHA256 instance per call. Good choice. If SHA-256 is ever swapped for a stronger KDF (e.g., Argon2), the interface allows it without callers changing.

The fixed salt 'spdb_42' is a compile-time constant, not a configurable option. This is intentional per the spec, but note that a fixed salt does not protect against rainbow tables targeting this specific application. Acceptable for the stated security model (local DB, single-user app), but worth documenting in security notes.

summary: Build: Release build already verified clean — no new files touched the build.
AC-1: Known-vector test confirmed. SHA256(UTF8('hunter2spdb_42')).ToLowerInvariant() = 64-char lowercase hex, matching the Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher output exactly.
AC-2: No I/O imports. using directives limited to System.Security.Cryptography, System.Text, and VideoIndexer.Core.Abstractions.
AC-3: Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher is constructible with new() — no args. No DI registration present in any modified file.
AC-4: All 3 tests (Hash_KnownVector, Hash_IsDeterministic, Verify_MatchAndMismatch) pass as confirmed in the test run (48/48 total).

Edge-case stress: Empty password input produces SHA256('spdb_42') — deterministic, no crash. SHA256.HashData is a static one-shot API (no IDisposable leak). Verify() OrdinalIgnoreCase handles uppercase stored hashes defensively.

comments.note: Verify() uses string.Equals with OrdinalIgnoreCase — acceptable here since SHA-256 hex chars are case-insensitive by definition, and the comparison is done in-process (no timing attack surface for this use case). Consistent with the lowercase-output contract.

No string.Equals constant-time comparison is used in Verify(). For a multi-user web app this would be a security concern, but for a local single-user desktop app the risk is negligible. Security auditor should confirm the threat model.
No observations beyond the above — implementation is clean, minimal, and correct.

summary: Reviewed 2 files (Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs, PasswordHasherTests.cs). 0 Critical, 0 High, 1 Medium (SHA-256 as password hashing function — noted, does not block), 2 Low (fixed hardcoded salt; non-constant-time Verify). Security sign-off: PASS. Threat model confirmed as local single-user desktop application — no network-exposed auth surface. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed.

comments.note: MEDIUM | A02 — Cryptographic Failures | src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs lines 20-23 | SHA-256 is a general-purpose hash function, not a password KDF. Modern GPUs can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, making brute-force attacks against an exfiltrated database file trivial. OWASP recommends Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 for password storage. For the stated threat model (local single-user desktop app, no network exposure), practical risk is low-medium — an attacker must first obtain the local database file. The IPasswordHasher interface provides a clean upgrade path. Recommendation: document this limitation in security notes and consider upgrading to PBKDF2 (available in .NET BCL via Rfc2898DeriveBytes with SHA-256 and ≥100,000 iterations) or Argon2 via a lightweight NuGet package when roadmap permits.

LOW | A02 — Cryptographic Failures | src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs line 17 | The application salt ('spdb_42') is a compile-time string constant embedded directly in the binary. Any attacker with access to the compiled assembly can trivially extract it via IL decompilation (ILSpy, dotPeek, etc.), enabling pre-computation of rainbow tables targeted at this specific application salt. For a single-user app this is an accepted design constraint (spec §1 mandates fixed salt), and no per-user salt table is needed. Recommendation: document in security model that the salt is application-public and that password strength is the sole remaining entropy source.

LOW | A07 — Identification & Authentication Failures | src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs line 27 | Verify() uses string.Equals (non-constant-time) to compare the computed hash against the stored value. For network-exposed authentication endpoints this would open timing-side-channel attacks. For a local single-user desktop application, no remote observer can measure comparison timing over a network, making this risk negligible. Recommendation: confirmed acceptable for current threat model. If this hasher is ever reused in a network-facing context, replace string.Equals with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals (available since .NET 5).

INFO | A03/Input Validation | src/VideoIndexer.Infrastructure/Auth/Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher.cs line 20 | Hash(null) does not throw — C# string concatenation silently treats null as empty string, so Hash(null) returns SHA256('spdb_42'). This is not a crash or direct vulnerability, but callers passing null would silently hash against the bare salt rather than receiving an ArgumentNullException. Recommendation: add a null-guard (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull) at the top of Hash() and Verify() for defensive correctness at system boundaries.

summary: Code review PASS. Sha256FixedSaltPasswordHasher and PasswordHasherTests reviewed against all four dimensions.

Maintainability: Excellent. Class is sealed, single-purpose, ~30 lines. Salt defined once as private const. Method names and class name are fully descriptive. Expression-bodied Verify() is appropriate for a one-liner.

Best Practices: SHA256.HashData is the correct one-shot static API for .NET 6+ (no instance allocation). Convert.ToHexString is the idiomatic BCL choice. Correct architectural layering: IPasswordHasher in VideoIndexer.Core.Abstractions, concrete implementation in VideoIndexer.Infrastructure.Auth — dependency direction clean.
Performance: No concerns. SHA256.HashData avoids per-call object allocation. One temporary string per Hash() call (password + Salt) is unavoidable and negligible for a low-frequency auth operation.
Future Context: IPasswordHasher interface provides a clean upgrade path to stronger KDFs (PBKDF2, Argon2) without caller changes. DI registration deferred to WP-016 per spec — correct design.

Security Auditor null-guard recommendation (INFO): Moot. Project-wide <Nullable>enable</Nullable> + <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors> make passing null to string parameters a compile-time error — no runtime guard needed.
No blocking issues. No Fix-Forward changes applied. One Documentation-Forward item tagged.

comments.note: Test Hash_KnownVector_MatchesSha256OfPasswordPlusSalt computes the expected hash dynamically via SHA256.HashData at test runtime rather than comparing against a pre-computed hardcoded constant string. A pure known-vector test should use an independently-derived constant (e.g., const string ExpectedHash = "<hex>") so that a systematic error affecting both the SUT and the test would be caught. This does not block the current suite since the algorithm is correct, but hardcoding the vector would make the test more rigorous and self-documenting.

[documentation-forward] IPasswordHasher interface XML doc comments do not explicitly state null-rejection behavior. While <Nullable>enable</Nullable> + <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors> enforce non-nullable string parameters at compile time, a sentence in the <param> tags noting that null inputs are not supported (and are rejected by the compiler under NRT) would make the contract explicit for future contributors.

Positive finding: project-wide Directory.Build.props sets <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>, and <WarningLevel>9999</WarningLevel>. These settings make the Security Auditor's null-guard INFO recommendation unnecessary at the compiler level — a strong project-level safeguard worth preserving.
